topics.h: How can a huge country like India fit on one page of your atlas? With a map!
p: A globe is a small round model of the Earth. It shows the true shape of the Earth and its continents and oceans.
A map is a flat drawing of the whole Earth or a part of it, like a city, a state or a country.
Maps are easy to carry and can show a small place in great detail, which a globe cannot.
Three key parts of a map are distance (scale), direction and symbols. A key or legend explains the symbols.
Physical maps show natural features like mountains and rivers; political maps show countries, states and cities; thematic maps show one theme, like rainfall or crops.

ex.q: On a map, 1 cm stands for 10 km. Two towns are 4 cm apart on the map. How far apart are they really?
st: The scale tells us 1 cm on the map = 10 km on the ground.
The towns are 4 cm apart, so multiply: 4 × 10 km.
ex.a: 40 km

topics.rl: Metro route maps, map apps on phones and the map of your school drawn for Sports Day are all maps with symbols and directions.

topics.h: If you stand facing the rising Sun, which direction is behind you? Let's find out!
p: The four main or cardinal directions are North (N), South (S), East (E) and West (W).
Between them are four intermediate directions: North-East (NE), South-East (SE), South-West (SW) and North-West (NW).
The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west, which helps us find directions outdoors.
A compass has a magnetic needle that always points to the north.
Most maps show north at the top, marked with an arrow and the letter N.

ex.q: Asha stands facing the rising Sun in the morning. Which direction is on her left?
st: The Sun rises in the east, so Asha is facing east.
When you face east, north is on your left and south is on your right.
West is behind her.
ex.a: North

topics.rl: Pilots, ship captains and trekkers in the Himalayas use compasses and maps so they never lose their way.

topics.h: Imagine drawing lines around a ball like belts. On the Earth, these belts are called latitudes!
p: Latitudes, also called parallels, are imaginary lines running east-west around the Earth, parallel to the Equator.
The Equator is the 0° latitude. It divides the Earth into the Northern and the Southern Hemisphere.
Latitudes are measured in degrees from 0° at the Equator to 90° at each Pole: 90°N is the North Pole and 90°S is the South Pole.
Important parallels: Tropic of Cancer (about 23.5°N), Tropic of Capricorn (about 23.5°S), Arctic Circle (about 66.5°N) and Antarctic Circle (about 66.5°S).
Places near the Equator are hot; places near the Poles are very cold. The Tropic of Cancer passes through the middle of India.

ex.q: A place is at 0° latitude. What can you say about it?
st: 0° latitude is the Equator.
The Equator gets the Sun's rays almost straight overhead through the year.
So the place is on the Equator and is usually hot.
ex.a: It lies on the Equator and is generally hot.

topics.rl: India lies fully in the Northern Hemisphere, and the Tropic of Cancer runs across states like Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and West Bengal.

topics.h: When it is noon in India, it is still early morning in London. How? The answer lies in longitudes!
p: Longitudes, also called meridians, are imaginary half-circles running from the North Pole to the South Pole.
The Prime Meridian is 0° longitude. It passes through Greenwich, near London. Longitudes go from 0° to 180° east and 180° west.
The Prime Meridian and the 180° line divide the Earth into the Eastern and Western Hemispheres.
The Earth spins once in about 24 hours, turning 360°. So it turns 15° in one hour, and 1° in 4 minutes.
Indian Standard Time (IST) is based on the 82°30'E (82.5°E) longitude. IST is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich time. Long ago, Indian astronomers used a prime meridian passing through Ujjain.

ex.q: It is 12 noon at Greenwich (0°). What time is it in India by IST?
st: India's standard meridian is 82.5°E, east of Greenwich.
The Earth turns 15° each hour, so 82.5 ÷ 15 = 5.5 hours, that is 5 hours 30 minutes.
Places to the east are ahead in time, so add 5 h 30 min to 12 noon.

topics.rl: When your cousin in London video-calls you after school at 5:30 pm IST in winter, it is only 12 noon for her! (In summer, London moves its clocks one hour ahead.)

topics.h: Seven giant pieces of land, and you live on the biggest one. Can you guess which?
p: A continent is a very large, continuous mass of land. There are seven continents.
From largest to smallest: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia.
Asia is the largest continent, and India is in Asia. Australia is the smallest and is also called an island continent.
Europe and Asia are joined together as one landmass (Eurasia); the Ural Mountains are often taken as the line between them.
Antarctica, around the South Pole, is covered with thick ice. It has no permanent towns, only research stations; India's stations there are Maitri and Bharati.

ex.q: Rohan says, 'Australia is a country, so it can't be a continent.' Is he right?
st: Australia is a country.
It is also a large landmass surrounded by water on all sides.
So it is counted as a continent, the smallest one, called an island continent.
ex.a: No. Australia is both a country and the smallest continent.

topics.rl: When you watch a cricket match between India and Australia, the two teams come from two different continents: Asia and Australia!

topics.h: If you could swim from Chennai going east, which ocean would you be in? Let's explore the oceans!
p: There are five oceans: the Pacific, the Atlantic, the Indian, the Southern and the Arctic.
The Pacific Ocean is the largest and the deepest ocean. Its deepest part is the Mariana Trench.
The Atlantic Ocean is the second largest and is shaped somewhat like the letter S.
The Indian Ocean is the only ocean named after a country: India. It lies south of India.
The Southern Ocean surrounds Antarctica, and the Arctic Ocean, the smallest, lies around the North Pole.

ex.q: Which ocean would a ship from Kochi first sail into?
st: Kochi is on the coast of Kerala, on the Arabian Sea.
The Arabian Sea is a part of the Indian Ocean.
So the ship sails into the Indian Ocean.
ex.a: The Indian Ocean

topics.rl: The fish you eat in coastal cities like Kochi, Visakhapatnam and Mumbai come from the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal, both parts of the Indian Ocean.

topics.h: Why do astronauts call the Earth the 'Blue Planet'? Look at how much water it has!
p: About 71% of the Earth's surface is covered with water and only about 29% is land.
About 97% of all the Earth's water is salty ocean water. Less than 3% is fresh water, and most of that is frozen as ice and glaciers.
The Northern Hemisphere has much more land than the Southern Hemisphere, which is mostly water.

Ocean water keeps moving: waves are mostly made by wind, tides are the regular rise and fall of the sea caused mainly by the pull of the Moon (and the Sun), and currents are large streams of water flowing in the oceans.
Oceans give us fish, salt and sea routes for ships, and they help control the Earth's climate.

ex.q: Out of every 100 parts of the Earth's surface, about 71 are water. How many parts are land?
st: The whole surface is 100 parts.
Water covers about 71 parts.
Land = 100 − 71 = 29 parts.
ex.a: About 29 parts (29%)

topics.rl: Salt from the sea is made by drying seawater in shallow pans along the coasts of Gujarat and Tamil Nadu.

topics.h: Why do people in Himachal Pradesh build their fields like giant staircases? Because they live on mountains!
p: A mountain is land that rises high above its surroundings, with steep slopes and often a pointed top called a peak.
A long chain of mountains is called a range. The Himalayas, to the north of India, are the highest mountain range in the world.
Mount Everest, in the Himalayas, is the highest peak in the world. Other ranges in India include the Aravalli and the Western Ghats.
High mountains have glaciers, which are slow-moving rivers of ice. Many rivers begin from them; the Ganga starts from the Gangotri glacier.
Life in the mountains: cold weather, thin air and steep land. People grow crops on terraces (step fields), keep animals like yaks and sheep, and many earn from tourism.

ex.q: Why do farmers in the mountains cut their fields into steps (terraces)?
st: Mountain slopes are steep.
On a steep slope, rainwater rushes down and washes away soil and seeds.
Flat steps slow the water and hold the soil, so crops can grow.
ex.a: Terraces make flat land on slopes and stop soil from being washed away.

topics.rl: Tea gardens in Darjeeling, apple orchards in Himachal Pradesh and yak herders in Ladakh are all part of mountain life in India.

topics.h: Imagine a giant table made of rock: high up, but flat on top. That's a plateau!
p: A plateau is a raised area of land with a fairly flat top and steep sides. It is often called a tableland.
The Deccan Plateau covers a large part of southern India. The Chota Nagpur Plateau lies mainly in Jharkhand.
The Tibetan Plateau, north of the Himalayas, is the highest plateau in the world.
Many plateaus are rich in minerals. The Chota Nagpur Plateau has large amounts of coal and iron ore.
Rivers flowing off the edges of plateaus often form beautiful waterfalls, and the black soil of parts of the Deccan is good for growing cotton.

ex.q: Why do many mines and steel plants come up in the Chota Nagpur Plateau?
st: Steel is made from iron ore, and coal is used to heat the furnaces.
The Chota Nagpur Plateau has large amounts of both iron ore and coal.
Factories save money and time when the raw materials are nearby.
ex.a: Because the plateau is rich in coal and iron ore.

topics.rl: Cities like Ranchi in Jharkhand and Pune and Bengaluru on the Deccan Plateau are built on plateaus.

topics.t: Plains and how landforms shape life
topics.h: Why do so many people live along the Ganga? Because plains are great for farming and building!
p: Plains are large stretches of low, flat land. Most are made by rivers that spread fine, fertile soil called alluvium.
The Indo-Gangetic plain in northern India, formed by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra and their tributaries, is one of the most fertile plains in the world.
Plains are good for farming, building houses and laying roads and railways, so they are usually crowded with people and cities.
Each landform shapes life: mountains give rivers, forests and tourism; plateaus give minerals; plains give food crops.
Deserts like the Thar in Rajasthan are dry, sandy lands where people keep camels, save rainwater and wear loose, light clothes.

ex.q: Why are there more big cities in plains than in mountains?
st: Plains are flat, so it is easy to build houses, roads and railways.
Their fertile soil grows plenty of food.
Rivers give water for drinking and farming, so many people settle there.
ex.a: Flat land, fertile soil and plenty of water make plains easy to live in.

topics.rl: The wheat in your roti and the rice in your plate likely grew on the plains of Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar or West Bengal.

topics.h: Is 500 BCE older or newer than 200 BCE? Counting time in history has a fun twist!
p: A timeline shows events in the order in which they happened, from earlier to later.
Most of the world today counts years using the Common Era. Years after the start of this count are written CE (Common Era); years before it are written BCE (Before Common Era).
Earlier, the same years were called AD and BC. CE is the same as AD, and BCE is the same as BC.
BCE years count backwards: 500 BCE came before 200 BCE. CE years count forwards: 200 CE came before 500 CE. There is no year zero; 1 BCE is followed directly by 1 CE.
A decade is 10 years, a century is 100 years and a millennium is 1,000 years. The 21st century runs from 2001 to 2100.

ex.q: Put these in order from oldest to newest: 300 CE, 600 BCE, 100 BCE, 1200 CE.
st: BCE years are older than all CE years.
Among BCE years, the bigger number is older: 600 BCE, then 100 BCE.
Among CE years, the smaller number is older: 300 CE, then 1200 CE.

topics.rl: Your birth year, the year your school was built and the year India became independent (1947) are all CE years you can put on your own family timeline.

topics.h: How do we know what people ate 2,000 years ago, when nobody had cameras? Historians are like detectives!
p: Historians find out about the past using sources, which are clues left behind from earlier times.
Archaeological sources are objects: tools, pots, beads, toys, coins, bones, buildings and paintings.
Written (literary) sources include manuscripts, handwritten long ago on palm leaves or the bark of the birch tree, and inscriptions, writings carved on stone or metal.
Oral traditions are songs, stories and sayings passed down by word of mouth from one generation to the next.
Historians compare many sources, check them carefully and then build a picture of what happened.

ex.q: A copper coin is found with a king's name and picture on it. What can a historian learn from it?
st: The name tells us who ruled.
The picture and words show the language and art of that time.
Where the coin is found shows how far trade or the kingdom reached.
ex.a: The ruler's name, the language and art of that time, and clues about trade.

topics.rl: Old family photos, your grandmother's recipes and the stories she tells are sources of your own family's history!

topics.h: Imagine digging carefully in the soil and finding a toy that a child played with 4,000 years ago!
p: Archaeology is the study of the past through the objects and buildings people left behind.
Archaeologists dig carefully at old sites. This careful digging is called excavation.
Usually, objects in deeper layers of soil are older and those in upper layers are newer.
Scientists can test materials like bones, seeds and wood to find out roughly how old they are.
The rock shelters of Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh have very old rock paintings of animals and people. They are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

ex.q: At a dig, an archaeologist finds a coin in the top layer and a stone tool in a much deeper layer. Which is probably older?
st: Soil and remains pile up over time, one layer on top of another.
Deeper layers were laid down earlier.
So the stone tool from the deeper layer is probably older.
ex.a: The stone tool.

topics.rl: When you visit a museum like the National Museum in New Delhi, many of the pots, seals and sculptures were found by archaeologists.

topics.h: Our country has had many beautiful names. The very first line of our Constitution uses two of them!
p: Article 1 of the Constitution of India says: 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.' So both India and Bharat are official names.
In the Rigveda, one of the oldest texts, the Bharatas are an important clan (group of people). The Rigveda also speaks of the land of seven rivers, 'Sapta Sindhu'.
The Vishnu Purana describes Bharatam as the land north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains, where the descendants of Bharata live.
Another old name is Jambudvipa, 'the island of the jambu (jamun) tree'. Emperor Ashoka used the word Jambudvipa in his inscriptions.
An inscription of King Kharavela at Hathigumpha in Odisha mentions 'Bharadhavasa', an early form of Bharatavarsha.

ex.q: The Vishnu Purana says Bharatam lies north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains. Which features are these?
st: South of India lie the seas: the Arabian Sea, the Indian Ocean and the Bay of Bengal.
North of India stand the snowy Himalayas.
So the text describes the land between the seas and the Himalayas.
ex.a: The ocean to the south and the Himalayas to the north.

topics.rl: The word Bharat is printed alongside India on our coins and passports, and we sing 'Bharat' in many patriotic songs.

topics.h: How did a river give its name to a whole country? Let's follow the Sindhu!
p: The Sindhu river (called the Indus in English) flows in the north-west of the subcontinent.
The ancient Persians said 'h' where Sanskrit has 's', so Sindhu became 'Hindu'. Here it was simply a name for the land and people of the Sindhu river region.
The Greeks dropped the 'h' sound, and 'Hindu' became 'Indos' or 'Indoi'. From this came the word 'India'.
Later, the Arabs called the land 'Al-Hind' and Persian writers called it 'Hindustan'.
The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, who travelled to India in the 7th century CE, called it 'Yindu'.

ex.q: How did the word 'India' come from the name of a river?
st: The river was called Sindhu.
Persians said 'Hindu' for Sindhu.
Greeks dropped the 'h' and said 'Indos', which later became 'India'.
ex.a: Sindhu → Hindu (Persian) → Indos (Greek) → India

topics.rl: The Indian Ocean, Indian cricket team and 'Hindustani' music all carry names that trace back to the Sindhu river.

rv.summary: Many names for our land came from the Sindhu river. The Persians said Hindu, the Greeks said Indos, which gave 'India'; Arabs said Al-Hind, Persian writers Hindustan, and Xuanzang Yindu.

topics.h: About 4,500 years ago, people in our part of the world were already living in planned cities with drains. Let's visit them!
p: The Harappan civilisation is one of the world's oldest. It is also called the Indus or Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation.
It is named after Harappa, the first of its cities to be excavated, in the 1920s. Harappa and Mohenjo-daro are now in Pakistan.
Important Harappan sites in India include Dholavira and Lothal (Gujarat), Kalibangan (Rajasthan) and Rakhigarhi (Haryana).
Its cities were at their peak from about 2600 BCE to about 1900 BCE, along the Sindhu (Indus) river and the Ghaggar-Hakra (often identified with the ancient Sarasvati).
Farmers grew wheat, barley and cotton and kept cattle; skilled crafts-people made pottery, beads, seals and bronze figures.

ex.q: Why is it called the 'Harappan' civilisation?
st: Archaeologists usually name a culture after the first site where it was found.
Harappa was the first city of this civilisation to be excavated.
So the whole civilisation was named after Harappa.
ex.a: Because Harappa was the first of its cities to be excavated.

topics.rl: You can see real Harappan seals, pots and the famous bronze 'dancing girl' figure in the National Museum, New Delhi.

rv.summary: The Harappan (Indus or Sindhu-Sarasvati) civilisation is one of the world's oldest, named after Harappa, the first city excavated. Its cities peaked from about 2600 to 1900 BCE.

topics.h: Covered drains, straight streets and bathrooms in houses, 4,500 years ago! Harappan engineers were brilliant planners.
p: Harappan cities had straight streets that crossed each other at right angles, in a grid pattern.
Many cities had a raised part called the citadel and a larger lower town where most people lived.
Houses were built of baked bricks of standard sizes. Many houses had a bathroom and some had their own well.
Covered drains ran along the streets to carry dirty water away, a sign of great care for cleanliness.
Mohenjo-daro had the Great Bath, a large, waterproofed tank. Dholavira had large reservoirs to store rainwater.

ex.q: Why were Harappan drains covered with bricks or stone?
st: Open drains can smell bad and spread disease.
Covering them kept dirt and waste out of sight and away from people.
Openings were left so the drains could be cleaned.
ex.a: To keep the city clean and healthy.

topics.rl: Modern Chandigarh, planned in grids with sectors, follows ideas similar to Harappan town planning!

topics.t: Trade, crafts and the end of the cities
topics.h: Harappan beads have been found far away in Mesopotamia (in present-day Iraq). How did they travel so far?
p: Harappans traded with distant lands such as Mesopotamia, using boats, ships and bullock carts.
They made square seals, often of a soft stone called steatite, with animals and a script. Seals may have been used to mark goods.
The Harappan script has not yet been read (deciphered), so we still don't know what the signs say.
Crafts-people made beads of carnelian (a red stone), pots, bronze figures like the 'dancing girl', and used standard stone weights for trade.
After about 1900 BCE the cities slowly declined. Likely reasons include changes in climate, rivers like the Ghaggar-Hakra drying up, and floods. People moved to smaller villages.

ex.q: Why might a Harappan trader have pressed a seal onto a clay tag tied to a sack of goods?
st: Seals carried a picture and some signs.
Pressing a seal on wet clay left a mark that showed who sent the goods.
This helped keep track of goods in trade.
ex.a: To mark the goods, showing where or whom they came from.

topics.rl: Shopkeepers today use stamps, labels and barcodes on packets, a little like Harappan seals.

topics.h: Imagine remembering thousands of verses perfectly, without a single book, and passing them on for thousands of years!
p: The Vedas are among the oldest texts of India, composed in an early form of Sanskrit.
There are four Vedas: the Rigveda, the Samaveda, the Yajurveda and the Atharvaveda. The Rigveda is the oldest.

The Vedas were passed on by word of mouth for a very long time. Students memorised them using careful methods of chanting. UNESCO has listed the tradition of Vedic chanting as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
The Rigveda has hymns to forces of nature, like Agni (fire) and Indra (linked with rain and thunder), and a famous line meaning 'Truth is one; the wise call it by many names'.
Later texts called the Upanishads discuss big questions, like 'Who am I?', through dialogues between teachers and students.

ex.q: How could the Vedas survive for so long when they were not written down for centuries?
st: Teachers recited the hymns and students repeated them exactly.
Special chanting patterns helped check that no word changed.
Each generation taught the next in the same way.
ex.a: They were memorised and passed down orally with great care.

topics.rl: Even today, the gurukula way of learning by listening and repeating is followed in some schools of Vedic chanting.

topics.h: A prince left his palace to find out why people suffer. Another teacher taught that even an ant's life matters. Who were they?
p: Siddhartha Gautama was born at Lumbini (in present-day Nepal). He left his comfortable life to understand the cause of suffering.
He gained enlightenment under a pipal tree (the Bodhi tree) at Bodh Gaya in Bihar and became the Buddha, the 'awakened one'. He gave his first sermon at Sarnath, near Varanasi.
The Buddha taught the Middle Path, avoiding extremes, along with the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path. He taught in the language of ordinary people.
Vardhamana Mahavira was the 24th tirthankara (great teacher) of Jainism. He was born near Vaishali in Bihar.
Jainism teaches ahimsa (non-violence to all living beings), truthfulness, not owning more than needed, and anekantavada: the idea that truth has many sides.

ex.q: Six friends each touch a different part of an elephant in the dark: one feels a trunk, one a tail, one a leg. Each describes 'the elephant' differently. Which Jain idea does this show?
st: Each friend is partly right, because each knows only one part.
None of them sees the whole elephant.
The Jain idea that truth has many sides and we should listen to other views is called anekantavada.
ex.a: Anekantavada: truth has many sides.

topics.rl: Many Jain families avoid harming even tiny insects, and Buddhist monasteries in Ladakh and Sikkim welcome visitors to learn about peace.

topics.h: In ancient India, thinkers loved to debate! Instead of one answer, many 'schools of thought' grew side by side.
p: A school of thought is a group of ideas about life and the world shared by teachers and their followers.
Ancient Indian philosophy developed several schools called darshanas, such as Sankhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa and Vedanta.
The Yoga school, linked with the sage Patanjali, teaches discipline of body and mind. Today, International Yoga Day is celebrated on 21 June.
Buddhism and Jainism also grew as separate schools of thought, with their own teachers and texts.
Folk and tribal traditions, like honouring nature, rivers, mountains and sacred groves of trees, are also important cultural roots. These ideas often mixed and learnt from each other.

ex.q: Why do we say India's cultural roots are like the roots of a banyan tree?
st: A banyan tree has many roots that hang down and grow into the ground.
India's culture also grew from many sources: the Vedas, Buddhism, Jainism, many darshanas and folk and tribal traditions.
All these roots support one big tree together.
ex.a: Because Indian culture grew from many different traditions that together support it.

topics.rl: Doing yoga at school, saying 'Namaste', and villagers protecting a sacred grove near their village are all living cultural roots.

topics.ch: Unity in Diversity, or 'Many in the One'
topics.t: Diversity of food, dress and festivals
topics.h: Breakfast in Chennai might be idli, in Amritsar it might be paratha, and in Kolkata luchi! India is a feast of diversity.
p: India is home to many languages. The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution lists 22 languages.

Food changes with climate and crops: rice is a main food in much of the south, east and north-east, while wheat rotis are common in the north and north-west. Millets like ragi, jowar and bajra are eaten in many states.
Clothes differ too: the saree is draped in many styles, like the nine-yard nauvari of Maharashtra; Assam has the mekhela chador, Kerala the mundu, and Kashmir the warm woollen phiran.
Harvest festivals are celebrated across India with different names: Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Bihu in Assam, Lohri in Punjab and Onam in Kerala.
This variety is called diversity. It grows from differences in climate, land, history and local traditions.

ex.q: Why do people in Kashmir wear a woollen phiran while people in Kerala often wear a light cotton mundu?
st: Kashmir has very cold winters, so warm woollen clothing is needed.
Kerala is warm and humid, so light cotton clothes feel comfortable.
So clothing grows from the local climate.
ex.a: Because of the difference in climate between the two regions.

topics.rl: Your class may have friends who speak Bengali, Tamil, Marathi or Hindi at home, and who celebrate different festivals. That's diversity in your own classroom!

rv.summary: India has great diversity in languages, food, clothes and festivals. This variety grows from differences in climate, land, history and local traditions.

topics.ch: Unity in Diversity, or 'Many in the One'
topics.h: Different colours of thread can be woven into one beautiful saree. India's unity is woven the same way!
p: Unity in diversity means that people with many differences also share common bonds. The chapter calls it 'many in the one'.
The Ramayana and the Mahabharata are told in many Indian languages: the Kamba Ramayanam in Tamil, the Ramcharitmanas of Tulsidas in Awadhi and the Krittivasi Ramayan in Bengali.
Many regions celebrate a new year around the middle of April with different names, such as Baisakhi, Bihu, Puthandu and Vishu.
Values like respecting elders, welcoming guests ('the guest is like god') and caring for nature are shared across regions.
The same idea can be dressed differently: the saree is one garment, but it is draped in many regional styles.

ex.q: Mira in Kolkata and Kiran in Chennai both know the story of Rama, but from different books in different languages. What does this show?
st: The story is the same at its heart.
Each region retold it in its own language and style.
So one shared story connects people across regions.
ex.a: A shared cultural thread: unity within diversity.

topics.rl: When your school celebrates a 'Unity Day' with dances and dishes from many states, you see many colours woven into one.

rv.summary: Unity in diversity means people with many differences share common bonds: 'many in the one'. Shared epics, mid-April new years, common values and the saree draped in many styles show this.

topics.h: Who cooks, who fixes the fan, who reads you bedtime stories? In a family, everyone has a part to play!
p: A family is the first group we belong to. It cares for us, protects us and teaches us values.
In a joint family, grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts and cousins live together. In a nuclear family, parents and their children live together.
Each member has roles and duties: earning, cooking, cleaning, shopping, caring for babies and elders, and helping with studies. Children help too, for example by tidying their things.
Sharing work fairly among everyone, whether boy, girl, man or woman, makes a family happy and strong.
Elders pass on stories, recipes, skills and traditions to younger members, and children often help elders with phones and new things.

ex.q: Ananya's mother works in an office, and her father cooks dinner on weekdays. Her grandmother helps her with homework. What does this show?
st: Different members are doing different jobs.
The jobs are shared based on time and skill, not on fixed ideas about who 'should' do them.
Everyone helps, so the family runs smoothly.
ex.a: Family members share roles and help each other.

topics.rl: When you lay the plates for dinner or water the plants at home, you are doing your role in the family.

topics.h: When a wedding happens in a village, neighbours lend chairs, cook together and decorate. That's community!
p: A community is a larger group of people who live near each other or share something in common, like a village, a neighbourhood or a housing society.
Communities help each other during festivals, weddings, illness and disasters like floods.
Important community values include cooperation, sharing, respect for others, honesty and caring for common spaces like parks, wells and ponds.
Communities also look after shared resources, such as cleaning a village pond or planting trees together.
An ancient Sanskrit saying, 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam', means 'the world is one family', extending these values to everyone.

ex.q: After heavy rains flood some homes in a village, what might the community do?
st: Neighbours give shelter to families whose homes are flooded.
People share food, clothes and help clean up.
Together they recover faster than any family could alone.
ex.a: They cooperate and share, helping everyone recover.

topics.rl: Resident welfare associations in cities, langars and community kitchens, and village clean-up drives are all communities in action.

topics.h: Who decides which side of the road we drive on, or when schools open? Someone has to make and run the rules. That's governance!
p: Governance is the way decisions are made, rules are put in place and a country, state or town is run for the good of everyone.
A government is the group of people and bodies that do this work. It makes laws, collects taxes and provides services like schools, hospitals, roads and safety.
Government has three organs (branches). The legislature makes laws. The executive puts laws into action. The judiciary (the courts) settles disputes and checks that laws are followed fairly.
Keeping these three powers separate, so that each checks the others, is called the separation of powers. It prevents misuse of power.
In India, Parliament is the legislature at the national level, and the Supreme Court is the highest court.

ex.q: A new law says everyone must wear a helmet on a two-wheeler. Which organ makes the law, which enforces it, and which decides a dispute about a fine?
st: The legislature (lawmakers) passes the helmet law.
The executive, through the traffic police, makes sure people follow it.
If someone disagrees with a fine, the judiciary (a court) decides.
ex.a: Legislature makes it, executive enforces it, judiciary settles disputes.

topics.rl: Traffic signals, school timings, vaccination drives and garbage collection are all examples of governance you see every day.

topics.h: Who fixes a broken streetlight, who runs the state's buses and who prints our currency? Different levels of government!
p: India has government at three main levels: the national (Union or Central) level, the state level and the local level.
The Union government looks after matters for the whole country, such as defence, currency, railways and relations with other countries.
State governments look after matters within a state, such as police, state hospitals and farming.
Local governments look after a village, town or city: drinking water, streetlights, cleanliness and local roads. In villages these are panchayats; in towns and cities, municipal bodies.
Each level has its own work, so that decisions are taken close to the people they affect.

ex.q: Who should repair a broken streetlight in your lane: the Union government, the state government or the local government?
st: A streetlight affects only one lane or ward.
Matters like streetlights and local cleanliness are handled by local government.
So the panchayat or municipal body should fix it.
ex.a: The local government.

topics.rl: You meet all three levels: your coins and train tickets come from the Union government, your state bus from the state government, and your street's garbage collection from the local body.

topics.h: In your class election, every student gets one vote. That's a mini democracy!
p: Democracy is a form of government in which people choose their leaders and have a say in how they are governed.
In India, people elect representatives who make decisions for them. This is called representative democracy.
Every Indian citizen aged 18 years or above can vote, whatever their religion, gender, caste, wealth or education. This is universal adult franchise.
Elections are held regularly. The Election Commission of India conducts elections to Parliament and to state legislatures.
India has a long tradition of discussion and assemblies. Ancient republics (ganas or sanghas), such as the Vajji (Vrijji) confederacy with its capital at Vaishali, took decisions in assemblies.

ex.q: Why is it fair that every adult gets exactly one vote, rich or poor?
st: In a democracy, every person is equal.
If some people got more votes, their wishes would count more than others'.
One person, one vote gives everyone an equal say.
ex.a: Because all citizens are equal, so each has an equal say.

topics.rl: On election day, adults in your family get a mark of indelible ink on a finger after voting. It shows they have voted.

topics.ch: Grassroots Democracy — Part 2: Local Government in Rural Areas
topics.h: The village handpump is broken. Who fixes it? The village's own government, the gram panchayat!
p: A gram sabha is made up of all the adults (18 years and above) of a village or group of villages whose names are on the voters' list.
The voters of the gram sabha elect the members of the gram panchayat (panches or ward members). Its head, the sarpanch (also called pradhan or mukhiya in some states), is also elected.
The gram panchayat looks after local needs: drinking water, village roads, drains, streetlights, cleanliness and keeping records like births and deaths.
In gram sabha meetings, villagers discuss plans, approve work and question the panchayat about how money was spent. This keeps the panchayat answerable to the people.
A panchayat secretary, appointed by the government, keeps records and calls meetings. Panchayats get money from local taxes and from government grants.

ex.q: Sunita, aged 19, lives in a village and her name is on the voters' list. Can she take part in the gram sabha?
st: Every adult aged 18 or above on the village voters' list is a member of the gram sabha.
Sunita is 19 and on the list.
So she is a member and can attend and speak.
ex.a: Yes, she is a member of the gram sabha.

topics.rl: When villages build a new pond, a school toilet or a concrete lane under a government scheme, the gram panchayat usually plans and supervises the work.

topics.ch: Grassroots Democracy — Part 2: Local Government in Rural Areas
topics.h: Panchayats are like a three-storey building: the village on the ground floor, the block in the middle and the district on top!
p: Panchayati raj is the system of local self-government in rural areas. It has three tiers (levels).
Tier 1 is the gram panchayat at the village level. Tier 2 is the panchayat samiti (also called block panchayat) at the block level. Tier 3 is the zila parishad at the district level.
The 73rd Amendment to the Constitution, passed in 1992, made panchayati raj a part of the Constitution. It came into force on 24 April 1993, which is why 24 April is National Panchayati Raj Day.
Panchayat elections are held every 5 years and are conducted by the State Election Commission.
At least one-third of the seats in panchayats are reserved for women; many states reserve half. Seats are also reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

ex.q: A road is needed to join several villages within one block. Which tier would most likely plan it?
st: A road within one village is the gram panchayat's work.
A road joining many villages of a block is bigger than one village.
So the panchayat samiti, at the block level, would plan it.
ex.a: The panchayat samiti (block level).

topics.rl: Many women sarpanches across India have led their villages in building toilets, saving water and improving schools, thanks to reserved seats.

topics.ch: Grassroots Democracy — Part 3: Local Government in Urban Areas
topics.h: Who collects the garbage from millions of homes in Mumbai every morning? The city's own government!
p: Towns and cities have their own local governments called urban local bodies or municipal bodies.
Big cities have a municipal corporation, smaller cities and towns have a municipal council (nagar palika), and areas changing from village to town have a nagar panchayat.
A municipal corporation is led by an elected mayor. Its daily work is run by a municipal commissioner, an officer appointed by the state government.
Municipal bodies provide water supply, drainage, garbage collection, streetlights, roads, parks, public toilets and birth and death certificates.
They get money from taxes such as property tax, from fees, and from government grants. The 74th Amendment (1992) gave urban local bodies a place in the Constitution.

ex.q: Delhi, a very large city, and a small hill town both need clean water. Which kind of municipal body would each most likely have?
st: Very large cities have a municipal corporation.
Smaller towns have a municipal council (nagar palika).
Areas just turning from village to town have a nagar panchayat.
ex.a: The large city has a municipal corporation; the small town has a municipal council.

topics.rl: When your family pays property tax or gets a birth certificate from the city office, they are dealing with the municipal body.

rv.summary: Towns and cities have municipal bodies: corporations for big cities, councils for smaller towns and nagar panchayats for areas becoming towns. They provide civic services and the 74th Amendment gave them a constitutional place.

topics.ch: Grassroots Democracy — Part 3: Local Government in Urban Areas
topics.h: A big city is like a giant pizza cut into slices. Each slice is a ward with its own elected councillor!
p: A city is divided into smaller areas called wards.
The people of each ward elect a representative called a councillor (also called a corporator in big cities).
The councillor raises the ward's problems, like broken roads or water shortage, in the meetings of the municipal body.

In larger cities, nearby wards are grouped under ward committees, which deal with local problems closer to the people. The 74th Amendment provides for ward committees in cities with a population of three lakh or more.
Citizens play a role too: paying taxes, keeping streets clean, segregating wet and dry waste, and reporting problems to the councillor or ward office.

ex.q: The drain in Arif's lane is blocked. What can his family do?
st: The drain is a local, ward-level problem.
They can complain to the ward office or their elected councillor, or use the city's helpline or app.
The municipal body then sends workers to clear it.
ex.a: Report it to the ward office or the ward councillor.

topics.rl: Many cities have helplines and apps where residents can post a photo of a pothole or an overflowing bin and track the repair.

rv.summary: A city is divided into wards, and each ward elects a councillor (corporator) to raise its problems. Ward committees handle local issues in bigger cities, and citizens help by paying taxes and keeping streets clean.

topics.h: Your mother cooks a delicious dinner and a restaurant chef cooks the same dish. Both are work, but one is paid. What's the difference?
p: Work done in return for money or payment in kind (like grain) is called an economic activity. Examples: a farmer selling vegetables, a teacher teaching, a tailor stitching clothes for customers.
Work done without payment, out of love, care, duty or to help others, is a non-economic activity. Examples: cooking for one's own family, caring for a sick grandparent, volunteering.
The same task can be economic or non-economic: a cook in a hotel is paid, while cooking for one's own family at home is not paid.
Unpaid work at home, like cooking, cleaning and caring, is very valuable. Families could not run without it, even though it earns no money.
Volunteering for the community, like helping at a community kitchen or a clean-up drive, is also valuable non-economic work.

ex.q: Kavya's father works as a driver for a company in the day and drives his own mother to the hospital in the evening. Which is economic activity?
st: Driving for the company earns him a salary, so it is economic activity.
Driving his mother is done out of care, without pay.
So the evening drive is non-economic activity.
ex.a: Driving for the company is economic; driving his mother is non-economic.

topics.rl: Volunteers who serve food at a community kitchen, and grandparents who look after grandchildren, are doing valuable unpaid work.

rv.summary: Economic activities are done for money or payment in kind; non-economic activities are done without pay out of love, care or duty. Unpaid work at home and volunteering are also very valuable.

topics.h: Imagine a city where sanitation workers stop for a week. Every job matters!
p: Dignity of labour means that every kind of honest work deserves respect, whether it is done with the hands or the mind.
Farmers, sanitation workers, cobblers, weavers, construction workers, doctors and engineers all keep society running.
No honest work is 'small'. Treating some jobs as low and others as high is unfair.
We show respect by thanking workers, speaking politely, paying fairly and not making extra mess for others to clean.
Many traditions in India value serving others through work, like sharing food in community kitchens where everyone, rich or poor, helps and eats together.

ex.q: Rohit's classmate laughs at a boy whose father is a cobbler. What should Rohit say?
st: A cobbler repairs shoes that people need every day.
His skill and honest work help many people.
Every honest job deserves respect, so laughing at it is unfair.
ex.a: That all honest work deserves respect: this is the dignity of labour.

topics.rl: When you thank the school sweeper, the bus driver or the canteen staff, you are practising the dignity of labour.

rv.summary: Dignity of labour means every kind of honest work deserves respect. Farmers, sanitation workers, cobblers, weavers and doctors all keep society running, and no honest work is 'small'.

topics.h: Every glass of milk, bowl of rice and pencil starts with someone using nature's gifts directly!
p: Primary activities use natural resources directly from nature.
Examples: farming, fishing, animal rearing (like dairy farming), forestry and mining.
Many people in India work in agriculture, growing crops like rice, wheat, pulses, cotton and sugarcane.
Fishing is important along the coasts of states like Kerala, Odisha, Gujarat and West Bengal; mining brings out coal, iron ore and other minerals.
Primary activities provide raw materials for factories and food for everyone.

ex.q: Is a fisherwoman in Kerala catching fish a primary activity?
st: She takes fish directly from the sea, a natural resource.
Nothing is being made in a factory.
So her work is a primary activity.
ex.a: Yes, fishing is a primary activity.

topics.rl: Dairy farmers in Gujarat and other states who sell milk to village dairy cooperatives are doing a primary activity.

rv.summary: Primary activities use natural resources directly from nature, such as farming, fishing, animal rearing, forestry and mining. They provide raw materials for factories and food for everyone.

topics.h: Raw cotton turns into your school uniform, and then a shop sells it to you. Two more kinds of work make it happen!
p: Secondary activities turn raw materials into new products. This is called manufacturing, and it often happens in factories or workshops.
Examples: making cloth from cotton, sugar from sugarcane, furniture from wood, and steel from iron ore. Building houses and bridges is also counted as secondary activity.
Tertiary activities provide services instead of making goods. Examples: transport, shops and trade, banking, teaching, healthcare, and phone and internet services.
So there are three sectors: primary (taking from nature), secondary (making goods) and tertiary (giving services).
Tertiary activities are also called services, and they help both the primary and the secondary sectors work.

ex.q: Is a doctor treating patients a primary, secondary or tertiary activity?
st: The doctor is not taking anything directly from nature, so it is not primary.
The doctor is not making a product, so it is not secondary.
The doctor gives a service, so it is tertiary.
ex.a: Tertiary activity.

topics.rl: The bus that takes you to school, the bank where your family saves money and the hospital nearby are all part of the tertiary (service) sector.

rv.summary: Secondary activities turn raw materials into new products (manufacturing), including construction. Tertiary activities provide services like transport, trade, banking, teaching and healthcare.

topics.h: How many people does it take to bring a packet of biscuits to your hand? Let's follow the chain!
p: The three sectors depend on one another. These connections are called linkages.
A wheat farmer (primary) grows wheat; a factory (secondary) turns it into flour and biscuits; trucks and shops (tertiary) carry and sell them to us.
If one link breaks, others are affected. A poor harvest of cotton means less cloth from mills and fewer clothes in shops.
Services like banking, transport, shops and phones help farmers and factories do their work.
Linkages also create jobs for many people at every step of the chain.

ex.q: Heavy rains destroy the sugarcane crop in a region. How might this affect a sweet shop in the nearby town?
st: Less sugarcane (primary) reaches the sugar mills.
The mills (secondary) make less sugar, so sugar may cost more.
The sweet shop (tertiary) pays more for sugar and may raise prices of sweets.
ex.a: Sweets may become costlier because the chain from farm to shop is linked.

topics.rl: The cotton in your T-shirt may have been grown in Gujarat or Maharashtra, spun in a mill, dyed, stitched, transported and sold in your local market.
